'A map is never neutral': meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias

The three creators of the Equal Earth projection — Tom Patterson, Bojan Šavrič, and Bernhard Jenny — describe their astonishment at the UN's near-universal adoption of their map, which more accurately represents Africa and all continents, and share how diplomatic complaints about borders crept into what was meant as a pure mathematical projection.

Key takeaways
  • The UN General Assembly voted 164-1 (US voting no, 6 abstentions) to adopt the Equal Earth projection, replacing Mercator on school walls and government websites
  • Tom Patterson, a retired US national parks cartographer, has been inundated with questions from governments and diplomats since the vote
  • Japan requested a revision because the map made the disputed Kuril Islands appear to belong to Russia; Ukraine abstained because Russian-occupied Crimea was shown in a different colour
  • The cartographers clarified the confusion: the UN resolution adopted a mathematical projection without borders — the border disputes arose from Patterson's annotated website version
  • Equal Earth was developed in 2018 by Patterson, Šavrič (software engineer), and Jenny (Monash University associate professor) as an alternative to both Mercator's size distortions and Gall-Peters' elongated appearance
  • Šavrič appreciated that the UN resolution does not ban Mercator or mandate a single replacement, instead promoting map literacy
  • Jenny noted the power of the name "Equal Earth" versus a hypothetical "Šavrič-Patterson-Jenny projection"
2026-09-18 The Guardian Source article

Amateur Astronomer Discovers 390-Million-Year-Old Crater on Google Maps

An amateur astronomer planning a camping trip on Google Maps spotted a near-perfect 15-mile ring in Quebec's Côte-Nord region that turned out to be a previously unrecorded 390-million-year-old meteorite impact crater — the first confirmed crater discovery by a member of the public.

Key takeaways
  • Joël Lapointe discovered the ring-shaped feature around Lake Marsal while browsing satellite maps for a camping trip in Quebec's Côte-Nord region in 2024
  • The crater, approximately 25 km in diameter, dates to the Devonian period (~390 million years ago) — over 100 million years before the first dinosaurs
  • Planetary geologist Gordon Osinski of Western University led a 2025 field expedition that confirmed the impact origin through shatter cones and impact melt rock
  • The team named the crater "Uhackatik" in consultation with the Innu Council of Ekuanitshit, on whose traditional land it lies
  • This is reportedly the first time a public sighting reported through the Impact Earth database has been confirmed as an impact crater
  • NASA's Earth Observatory published a Landsat 8 view of the structure, with the circular outline faintly visible around the lake
  • Geologists estimate hundreds more impact craters remain unidentified on Earth, many under sediment, ice, or ocean
2026-09-17 Futura Sciences Source article

How AI Object Detection Is Changing What "Imagery" Means

Geo Week News examines how AI object detection is transforming satellite imagery from pictures that humans look at into queryable spatial databases, drawing an analogy to how full-text search changed our relationship with documents.

Key takeaways
  • Object detection models can now identify discrete objects (vehicles, aircraft, ships, buildings, bridges, storage tanks) in satellite imagery with precision rivaling human performance
  • The overhead top-down perspective of satellite imagery is well-suited for detection architectures: objects don't occlude each other as in ground photos, lighting is more uniform, and the nadir view provides a consistent frame of reference
  • Each detection outputs a bounding box, class label, and confidence score, turning imagery into a queryable spatial database
  • Earth observation foundation models like NASA/IBM's Prithvi and Allen Institute's SatlasPretrain use pre-training on vast unlabeled archives followed by fine-tuning for specific tasks
  • Temporal object detection represents the next frontier: tracking when objects appear, how long they stay, and where they go — converting counts into patterns
  • The shift parallels how full-text search transformed documents from things to read into things to query
2026-09-17 Geo Week News Source article

A fairer world map – but old borders creep back in

The Lowy Institute analyzes how the UN's "Correct the Map" resolution, intended to replace the Mercator projection with equal-area alternatives, has become entangled in sovereignty disputes as countries object to how the new maps depict contested territories.

Key takeaways
  • The UN General Assembly voted 164-1 in favor of the "Correct the Map" resolution, with the United States the sole opponent and six abstentions (Ukraine, Moldova, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Serbia)
  • The resolution encourages governments, schools, and tech companies to adopt equal-area projections like Equal Earth that show accurate relative sizes of landmasses
  • Ukraine abstained because the Equal Earth map depicts Crimea as part of Russian territory; Moldova abstained in solidarity with Ukraine
  • India and Japan voted in favor but subsequently raised concerns about how the map depicts Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Arunachal Pradesh, and the Kuril Islands respectively
  • The US argued the resolution is part of a "radical ideological project" and questioned why the UN was devoting attention to a 16th-century map
  • The resolution is non-binding, and the UN's own emblem uses an azimuthal equidistant projection centered on the North Pole, not an equal-area projection
2026-09-18 Abhinandan Kumar / Lowy Institute Source article

New World Map Makes Africa Look Bigger: What's the Fuss About? Cartographers Explain

Cartographers Jack Swab and Derek Alderman explain the UN's endorsement of the Equal Earth projection, why the Mercator map distorts Africa's true size, how the new projection works, and why the US was the lone "no" vote against the resolution.

Key takeaways
  • The UN passed a non-binding resolution endorsing the Equal Earth projection over the Mercator projection, which exaggerates land towards the poles by 2-14x
  • The Mercator projection remains useful for navigation (preserving compass bearings), which is why Google Maps and Apple Maps still use it
  • The Equal Earth projection minimizes distortions of continental sizes, making it better for educational, public communication, and policy purposes
  • Map-making is decentralized — no single authority regulates which projection is used; the UN endorsement is symbolic, not mandatory
  • The US was the only "no" vote, calling the resolution a "radical and ideological project" and objecting to language linking Mercator's distortions to colonial legacies
  • Ukraine raised concerns over the depiction of Crimea, while other nations raised contested territory issues — but these were geopolitical posturing, not map issues
  • African nations framed the resolution as "cognitive justice" — correcting the mental map that equates size with power and importance

Google Maps Is Now Terrible: Explained

The Drive explains why Google Maps and similar navigation apps have gotten worse at saving time: mass adoption of GPS routing means too many users are sent down the same alternate routes, creating a Nash equilibrium where individual optimization degrades collective outcomes — and there is no easy fix.

Key takeaways
  • An estimated 7 billion devices worldwide rely on GPS, from phones to golf balls
  • A 2019 study found that between 2007 and 2017, services like Google Maps saved 52 billion gallons of fuel and a trillion miles through more efficient routing
  • GPS adoption has generated an estimated $1.4 trillion in economic benefits since the 1980s
  • The core problem: routing apps don't track how many users they've sent on a given route and can't know where competitor services are sending users
  • When everyone uses the same app to avoid traffic, alternate routes become congested too, negating the benefit
  • This creates a Nash equilibrium where individual route optimization degrades collective traffic outcomes
  • There is no simple solution — the problem is structural to how decentralized routing works at scale
